resources.string: How parietal cells secrete stomach acid
A qualitative view of normal human stomach digestion, following one parietal cell in a gastric gland. The cutaway, feedback loop, timing and particle counts are schematic.
Find a parietal cell in a gastric gland

In the body of the stomach, gastric glands open into the stomach cavity through gastric pits. The highlight locates one parietal cell along a gland. Its acid-secreting side opens into the gland, away from nearby blood vessels.
A local signal readies the cell

Histamine from a nearby cell is one signal for acid secretion. It binds on the blood-facing side of the parietal cell. Inside the cell, membranes carrying proton pumps join the apical membrane lining the canaliculus, a narrow passage open to the gland lumen.
The pump exchanges protons for potassium
At the canaliculus, the proton pump uses energy from ATP to move protons (H⁺) out of the cell and potassium ions (K⁺) in. Both movements are shown at the same pump on the side facing the gland lumen.
Chloride joins protons in the lumen

Chloride ions (Cl⁻) pass through a separate channel into the same passage. The protons and chloride form the hydrochloric acid component of gastric juice. This juice reaches the stomach cavity, where the acidic environment helps digest proteins.

As stomach contents become more acidic, feedback signals including somatostatin restrain gastrin release. With less stimulation from gastrin, parietal cells secrete less acid. The diagram traces one pathway rather than showing all the signals involved.
